Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G5. Prompting is static, generic, and domain-agnostic: The text encoder is kept frozen, and the prompts consist of hand-crafted normal/abnormal state descriptions averaged over 35 ImageNet templates. This design presumes a single, universal visual-language concept of “normal” and “abnormal” that holds uniformly across imaging modalities, and it omits instance-adaptive, visually conditioned, or hybrid prompting strategies. No prompt-sensitivity analysis is provided.
- G7. Normal/anomaly disentanglement and distributional asymmetry are not made explicit: The dual- adapter design separates anomaly-classification and anomaly-segmentation features, but it does not explicitly model the compact distribution of normal samples against the comparatively diverse distribution of abnormal samples. The method relies on shared adapted features and a few-shot normal memory bank without routing mechanisms, dual normal/abnormal pathways, or many-to- one, SigLIP-style regularization.
- G13. Scalability, memory, and privacy considerations are unaddressed: The method uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone and trains six separate leave-one-out models for 50 epochs each on a single RTX 3090 GPU; training and inference time, memory footprint, and parameter counts are not reported. The term “lightweight” refers only to the adapters, not to the overall system. The few-shot memory bank grows with K and with spatial resolution, yet retrieval cost and the privacy and governance implications of storing patient-derived features are not analyzed. Downscaling to a 240 × 240 resolution and processing volumetric data as 2D slices may cause small lesions and broader 3D CT/MRI context to be lost.
